clue.text: Crazy fool had the quinoa?

indicators.note: something crazy is deranged and out of order, so the letters beside it are jumbled

parts.note: three words taken as written, ten letters in all

explanation.surface: Someone mocks a diner who ordered the trendy grain dish as a crazy fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fool had the' reads as the start of a sentence about a diner, but it is the letter supply; the question mark shows the definition is by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Quinoa is a grain sold and eaten as a wholesome, nutritious product, one example of the category.

clue.text: Perhaps displays impatience, for beer's essential

definitions.meaning: first meaning: jumps from foot to foot, as someone restless might
second meaning: the dried flowers used to flavour and bitter beer

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a drinker impatient for a pint; the verb sense of jumping on one foot is only loosely impatient, hence 'Perhaps'.
explanation.definitionFit: Brewers add the flower cones of a climbing plant for bitterness and aroma, making them a core ingredient of ale.

clue.text: Performs part of New Testament

definitions.meaning: first meaning: plays a role on stage
second meaning: the book of the Apostles, fifth in the Christian scriptures

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as an actor taking a biblical role, but the verb and the book title are separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The Acts of the Apostles is a book of the Christian Bible, and to do this is to play a stage role.

clue.text: Recklessly, rather soon, Jack's accepted problematic gift

indicators.note: what is accepted is taken in, so one piece is let inside another
acting recklessly means without care or order, so the letters are thrown into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
J is the abbreviation for jack in a pack of cards

explanation.surface: Jack rashly and too hastily accepted a present that turned out to be trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: The J goes into the other letters first, then all eleven are rearranged into TROJAN HORSE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greeks left a wooden statue for Troy that concealed soldiers, so the phrase now means any seemingly welcome offering hiding danger.

clue.text: Pals seen as weekend begins?

parts.note: the weekend comes after Friday, abbreviated FRI
the weekend begins when that day finishes

explanation.surface: Your mates turn up just as the weekend gets going.
explanation.walkthrough: The weekend begins when FRI ENDS, which run together as FRIENDS; the question mark flags this roundabout reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Pals are companions you like and trust, the everyday synonym for close acquaintances.

clue.text: Add one's voice again, almost too late — bravo!

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: overdue means too late; its final E is lost
B is bravo in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A singer re-records a vocal, cheered on as the session runs late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bravo' looks like applause but is the radio code word for the letter B.
explanation.definitionFit: To overdub is to record an additional layer, such as a vocal track, over an existing recording.

clue.text: An additional additional note, as may be found on your phone

definitions.text: may be found on your phone

parts.note: the article as a single letter
PS is a postscript, an additional note; PPS adds one after that

explanation.surface: A text message with a second afterthought tacked on, the sort of thing on your phone.
explanation.walkthrough: PPS stands for post-postscript, a note added after the first postscript, hence the doubled 'additional'.
explanation.definitionFit: Smartphones carry downloaded software programs, the short word for applications.

clue.text: I take it before supper to begin with? Um, very well

parts.note: the prefix meaning before

indicators.note: what comes to begin with is the opening, so only the first letter is kept

parts.note: opening letter of the meal
taken as written
doing something ably is doing it very well

explanation.surface: Someone hesitantly asks whether a pill should be taken before the evening meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I take it' sounds like taking medicine but is the definition, a phrase for supposing.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases express a supposition or assumption made without certain proof, so they are interchangeable in speech.

clue.text: Summer garb, close-fitting, topless: vision, but not perfect

indicators.note: without a top means the head of the word is removed, its first letter

parts.note: short trousers worn in hot weather
tight means close-fitting; the T at its top goes

explanation.surface: Skimpy, tight summer clothing, going topless, catches the eye of an onlooker.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue the top of a word is its first letter, so 'topless' removes the T.
explanation.definitionFit: Myopia is a defect where distant things look blurred, so eyesight falls short of ideal.

clue.text: Often visits and scorns

definitions.meaning: first meaning: is a regular customer of a shop or restaurant

explanation.walkthrough: The two meanings pull in opposite directions, a loyal regular and a sneering superior, which hides the single word.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means both to frequent a business as a customer and to talk down to someone condescendingly.

clue.text: Protest when flipping Everyman welcomed into party

indicators.note: a guest welcomed into a place is inside it, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: a do is an informal British word for a party

indicators.note: to flip something is to turn it over, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: the setter refers to themself, giving ME; the letters also sit backwards at the end of 'welcomed', a coincidence

explanation.surface: A protest breaks out when the setter, flipping out, is let into a party.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often clue themselves by pseudonym, so Everyman means ME; a do is a party.
explanation.definitionFit: A demo is the short form of demonstration, a public march or rally opposing something.

clue.text: Acquired, or was able to acquire, bread?

definitions.text: Acquired, or was able to acquire, bread?

parts.note: surface reading: someone obtained a loaf, or its outer part
setter's reading: bread is slang for money, so this is making enough to live on

explanation.walkthrough: The clue offers the literal picture of getting a piece of bread and the idiom for making a modest living; both fit the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The British idiom means making just enough money to get by, and bread is old slang for cash.

clue.text: Nick castled unwisely, cause of abrupt end in board game

definitions.text: cause of abrupt end in board game

indicators.note: doing something unwisely means doing it wrongly, so the letters come out in the wrong order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Nick made a rash castling move in chess, which cost him the game.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points to chess, but the board game is Cluedo (Clue in North America), where a candlestick is one of the murder weapons.
explanation.definitionFit: In the murder-mystery game, the victim may have been killed with this holder for a taper, one of six weapons.

clue.text: Rough grittiness, displaying most fibre

indicators.note: rough means crude and unpolished, so the letters are roughed up into another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Coarse, gritty food shows off the greatest amount of roughage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rough' reads as describing the grittiness, but it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Stringy food is full of tough threads, so the superlative describes whatever is most full of such strands.

clue.text: Rewarding academic, second 'character' from High Table

parts.note: short for professor

indicators.note: a character is a letter, so the second one is taken from the word that follows

parts.note: second letter of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: A don is pleased when a colleague who is quite a character comes over from High Table.
explanation.walkthrough: High Table is where senior fellows dine in an Oxbridge college; the quotation marks warn that 'character' means a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something rewarding brings gain or benefit, and a profitable venture yields a financial return.

clue.text: Lights a fire under section of concert orchestra

indicators.note: a section is a slice cut from something larger, so the letters are a run within the next words

parts.note: the run starts with the last letter of the first word

explanation.surface: A conductor stirs up part of the orchestra, lighting a fire under them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Section' suits an orchestra, where strings and brass are sections, which disguises its role.
explanation.definitionFit: To torch something is to set it ablaze deliberately, as an arsonist does to a building.

clue.text: Indonesian island adopting English language

indicators.note: to adopt is to take in and give a home, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: the resort island east of Java
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: An island in Indonesia begins using English as a language.
explanation.walkthrough: The Indonesian island points to a Southeast Asian tongue, but the answer is spoken in Bangladesh and West Bengal.
explanation.definitionFit: Bengali is the main tongue of Bangladesh and the Indian state of West Bengal, one of the world's most widely spoken.

clue.text: Conclude with refusal: hell!

parts.note: to infer is to conclude from evidence
a refusal is a no

explanation.surface: Someone ends a conversation by refusing and swearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hell!' looks like an exclamation of frustration but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Dante's poem named the underworld of the damned this way, and the word now means a blazing place of torment.

clue.text: Lear's daughter, stuck between ducks, leaves

indicators.note: something stuck between two things sits in the middle, flanked on each side

parts.note: a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, shaped like O; two of them
Regan is one of King Lear's daughters in Shakespeare

explanation.surface: One of King Lear's daughters, trapped between two ducks, walks off.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a duck is a score of zero, so ducks give two Os; 'leaves' seems to be a verb but is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The herb is a Mediterranean plant whose dried foliage is used for seasoning, especially in Italian cooking.

clue.text: Distressing figure in Old Testament?

parts.note: surface reading: an upsetting or harrowing character in scripture
setter's reading: dis-tressing, removing someone's locks of hair

explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Distressing' as dis-tressing, cutting off tresses: the Philistine woman had Samson's hair shorn, stripping his strength.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Book of Judges she betrayed Samson by having his hair cut while he slept, taking his strength.

clue.text: Unconventional artist painted a daïs turquoise in parts

indicators.note: the letters come in parts, spread across several words rather than one

parts.note: a run across four words, reading through the diaeresis as a plain I

explanation.surface: An eccentric painter coated a platform turquoise in places.
explanation.walkthrough: The diaeresis on the I of daïs just marks a separate syllable and is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: Dada was an early twentieth-century anti-art movement, and its members rejected conventional aesthetics.

clue.text: Sat idly; doctor had urged test

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters are altered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A patient lazed about after the physician had pressed for a medical test.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' reads as the physician, but it is a verb meaning to tamper.
explanation.definitionFit: An object left unused for a long time accumulates grime, so the idiom means remained neglected and inactive.

clue.text: Couple, trim (we're told)

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

parts.note: to pare is to trim away the edges

explanation.surface: A couple are trim, or so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: PARE and PAIR are pronounced identically.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean two things or people considered together as a set.

clue.text: Regularly — often — tea is cheese

indicators.note: at regular intervals means every other letter, a steady skip pattern

parts.note: even-position letters across both words

explanation.surface: Someone declares that tea is often, regularly, a matter of cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: The count runs straight through both words, taking the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Feta is a crumbly white Greek variety made from sheep's or goat's milk.

clue.text: Exiled loser Bonaparte's abode, primarily?

indicators.note: primarily means in the first place, so the first letter of each word is kept

parts.note: initial letters of the four words

explanation.surface: Where the defeated Napoleon lived after being banished.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue both supplies the letters and describes the answer, so it is an all-in-one.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon was banished in 1814 to this Mediterranean island off Tuscany before escaping for the Hundred Days.

clue.text: Breaching front, head of infantry landed; at ease

indicators.note: to breach a wall is to break through into it, so the following pieces go inside

parts.note: the face is the front of something

indicators.note: the head is the top, so only the first letter is taken

parts.note: first letter
lit means landed, as a bird alights
taken as written

explanation.surface: Soldiers break through the enemy line, the leading troops land, and all is calm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At ease' looks like a military order but splits: 'at' joins the inserted pieces and 'ease' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To facilitate a task is to make it simpler or smoother, the verb sense of removing difficulty.

clue.text: Beating a retreat, run into swarm

indicators.note: retreating means going back the way you came, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: to run into someone is to meet them

explanation.surface: Fleeing troops collide with a swarming crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run into' suggests collision, but it is the phrase for encountering someone by chance.
explanation.definitionFit: To teem is to be full of moving creatures, as a pond swarms with fish.

clue.text: Ask her out, possibly to take in a little open country

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it inside, so a piece is included within the rest
possibly signals one of several arrangements, so the letters may be reordered

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: just a little of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter

explanation.surface: A suitor considers asking a woman out to see some open countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Open country' reads as a phrase for landscape; 'open' gives one letter and 'country' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Republic of Korea is the nation occupying the southern half of the Korean peninsula.
